title: Sales Tax by State: 2026 Rates and Rankings
summary: Compare 2026 sales tax rates by state, including state, local, and combined rates, plus rankings of the highest and lowest states and the 5 with no sales tax.
body_markdown:
In the United States, 45 states plus Washington, D.C. charge sales tax. Only Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon don’t have statewide sales tax.


In states that do have sales tax, rates vary dramatically, from a combined state and local tax rate as high as 12.625% in Arkansas to as low as 4.5% in Hawaii.

## Which state has the highest sales tax?


**Indiana, Mississippi, Rhode Island, and Tennessee** tie for the highest state sales tax rate at 7%.


Some areas also have local sales taxes. **Arkansas** has the highest possible combined sales tax rate in the town of[Gillham, Arkansas](https://www.dfa.arkansas.gov/office/taxes/excise-tax-administration/sales-use-tax/sales-use-tax-rates/city-and-county-sales-use-tax-rates/) , at 12.625%.


### Highest combined sales tax rates


The table below shows the states with the highest combined rates.

This table demonstrates the impact of local tax rules. Both Colorado and Alabama have relatively low statewide rates. However, costly local taxes mean some areas in Colorado and Alabama have some of the country's highest combined rates.


Local sales tax rates often apply only in specific cities, counties, or special districts. They do not apply statewide.


For example, buyers in York, Alabama, pay a combined 12% rate: 4% state + 4%[Sumter County](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Sumter-County_20251124.pdf) + 4% city. Customers pay that 12% only on purchases in York, not in other parts of Alabama, where the combined rate can be as low as 4%.


### Highest state sales tax rates


In total, 25 U.S. locations have rates of 6% or higher. Four states are tied for the highest state sales tax rate. These rates apply statewide.

Remember, high statewide rates don't always mean high combined rates. For example, Indiana and Rhode Island charge no local sales tax, so the maximum any buyer pays is 7%. As a result, Rhode Island and Indiana rank 32nd for the maximum combined rate.


By contrast, Tennessee areas charge local rates ranging from 1.5% to 2.75%, so the state ranks 13th for the maximum combined rate.


California also doesn't make the list of states with the highest statewide rates, despite a combined minimum rate of 7.25%. That's because the mandatory statewide rate is only 6%. High local taxes across the state are why customers pay so much in sales tax.


## Which state has the lowest sales tax?


In the U.S., five states charge no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon.


Among states that charge sales tax, Nevada has the lowest state-only rate at 2%, while Hawaii has the lowest combined rate at 4.5%.

Hawaii shoppers pay the least sales tax (4.5% max statewide) because the statewide rate is 4% and local rates top out at 0.5%.


However, Hawaii doesn't have a traditional sales tax. It charges a[General Excise Tax (GET)](https://tax.hawaii.gov/get/) . The GET taxes businesses' gross receipts, not buyers, and applies to nearly all business activity, including services and rents. So, a low rate doesn't mean a light tax.


Because companies usually pass this cost on to consumers, it is often treated like a sales tax and appears on customer receipts.


It’s also worth noting that a low state rate doesn't necessarily mean a low combined rate. While Nevada's statewide rate is just 2%, mandatory local taxes mean the minimum combined rate any customer pays anywhere in Nevada is 6.85%.


Colorado also has a very low statewide rate of 2.9%, but local rates go as high as 9.1%, making the highest combined rate 12%. This is tied for the second-highest in the country.


Similarly, Alaska charges no state sales tax, but local rates go as high as 7.85%, giving it the 30th-highest combined rate.


Because local taxes are often very high, you can't look only at statewide taxes when determining if a state is tax-friendly.


## States with no sales tax


Five U.S. states don’t charge a statewide sales tax. These include Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon.


The absence of a statewide sales tax does not mean customers pay no sales tax. In all five states, taxes are charged on certain purchases or levied on merchants in other ways.


- [Alaska:](https://www.numeral.com/blog/alaska-sales-tax-guide) No statewide tax, but local governments levy sales taxes up to 7.85%.
- [Delaware:](https://www.numeral.com/blog/delaware-sales-tax-guide) Businesses pay a gross receipts tax on total gross revenues.
- [Montana:](https://www.numeral.com/blog/montana-sales-tax-guide) Some resort areas levy local resort taxes.
- [New Hampshire:](https://www.numeral.com/blog/new-hampshire-sales-tax-guide) Meals, rooms, and rental cars may be taxed.
- [Oregon:](https://www.numeral.com/blog/oregon-sales-tax-guide) Businesses with more than $1 million in commercial activity pay a Corporate Activity Tax (CAT), a gross-receipts tax rather than a sales tax.


Remote sellers may be obligated to charge these taxes on relevant sales. In Alaska, for example, the[Alaska Remote Sellers Sales Tax Commission](https://arsstc.org/) coordinates local sales tax collection for remote sellers and marketplace facilitators.


Sellers that are based in states that do not charge sales tax are also expected to comply with sales tax rules in other jurisdictions. They must understand rules for[physical](https://www.numeral.com/blog/physical-nexus) and[economic nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/economic-nexus) in any location where they have a physical presence or local customers.


Once a remote seller establishes nexus in another state, they must register, file, and remit according to local requirements.


## Who sets sales tax rates: Is sales tax federal or state?


The United States has no federal sales tax. States and localities set all sales tax rules. Specifically:


- State legislatures set the statewide rate and decide which items are taxable.
- Counties and cities can establish a local sales tax rate if the state allows it. Often, this requires voter approval.
- Special districts may also be created. In these districts, taxes fund specific initiatives such as schools, public safety, or transportation.


In certain states, individual localities can establish and operate their own sales tax systems without input from the state legislature. For example, in Colorado,[home rule](https://www.numeral.com/blog/home-rule-states-sales-tax) authorizes localities to set their own tax rules, and in[Louisiana](https://www.numeral.com/blog/louisiana-sales-tax-guide) , parishes set theirs.


[Alabama](https://taxfoundation.org/statetaxindex/states/alabama/) also lets local governments and independent tax boards administer their own tax system, though the state has a unified tax base. And Alaska lets localities set their own sales tax rates despite having no statewide tax.


Sellers, including remote sellers, must ensure they comply with both statewide and local rules.


Local and state rates can also change throughout the year, although many states allow these changes to take effect only at the start of a calendar quarter. For example, under the[Texas state tax administration rules](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/?tab=1&code=TX&chapter=TX.321&artSec=) , if a city or county votes to implement a local sales tax change:


- The local jurisdiction must officially notify the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.
- The state enforces a full calendar-quarter waiting period after the Comptroller receives notice.
- The tax change becomes effective on the first day of the next calendar quarter.


### Recent sales tax rate changes


Frequent changes to state tax rules complicate compliance for merchants, especially those that must follow sales tax rules in multiple jurisdictions. For example, here are some recent state and local changes:


- [California SB 122](https://www.numeral.com/blog/california-sb-122) makes most prewritten software and SaaS taxable starting Jan. 1, 2027.
- [Illinois](https://tax.illinois.gov/research/publications/bulletins/fy-2026-03.html) eliminated its 1% state sales tax on groceries effective Jan. 1, 2026. Many local governments responded by adding their own grocery tax.
- Multiple Georgia counties raised rates through the new[Floating Local Option Sales Tax](https://cedr.gatech.edu/georgia-flost-property-tax-relief-guide/) , which allows municipalities to offer property tax relief.
- [Louisiana](https://dam.ldr.la.gov/lawspolicies/RIB%2025-007%20-%20State%20Sales%20Tax%20Rate.pdf) raised its statewide rate from 4.45% to 5% in January 2025.
- South Dakota's 2023 rate cut to 4.2% is set to expire in July 2027, returning the state rate to 4.5%. A[2026 bill](https://www.kotatv.com/2026/02/20/effort-keep-south-dakotas-reduced-sales-tax-rate-permanent-stalls-sen-deibert-weighs/) to make the cut permanent failed in the state Senate.


## Why local sales tax rates vary and how to find your exact rate


Sales tax rates vary because state and local governments can levy their own sales tax. This local freedom creates significant complexities for merchants.


For example, a seller in Colorado may be required to collect sales tax ranging from 2.9% to 12% depending on the buyer's location. Sellers must understand all of the taxes that apply within the taxing jurisdiction of each customer. This could potentially include:


- State rates
- County rates
- City rates
- Special district rates


The sum of these four rates is the applicable rate. Unfortunately, sellers must charge the correct tax for *each* address. As of 2020, the U.S. has more than[11,000 standard sales tax jurisdictions](https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-sales-tax-jurisdictions-in-the-us-2020/) , and their boundaries don't follow ZIP codes.


This means a seller selling to two buyers in the same ZIP code may have to charge different sales tax rates. For example, in the 80111 ZIP code in Greenwood Village, portions of the ZIP code fall within[Greenwood Village](https://greenwoodvillage.com/1465/Examples) boundaries and are subject to city taxes that don't apply to unincorporated areas of the county.


Sellers can identify the exact rate that applies by using state lookup tools such as the[Washington Department of Revenue](https://dor.wa.gov/) , the[California Department of Tax and Fee Administration](https://www.cdtfa.ca.gov/) , or the[Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/) .


Of course, looking up rates for each individual sale isn't practical.


Many merchants use tax calculation software that automatically calculates the correct tax in real time on every order based on location and item. For example, Numeral's[tax engine](https://www.numeral.com/product/api) calculates rates at the rooftop level using coordinate-level precision, rather than relying on ZIP codes.


## How to calculate sales tax on a sale


There is a simple formula used to calculate sales tax on a sale:


**Sales Price x Combined Rate = Sales Tax Owed**


Here is how this works in practice:


- You sell an $86.50 ceramic planter.
- The buyer is located in an area with a combined 9.1% rate.
- Multiply $86.50 x 9.1% to determine that you must collect $7.87 in sales tax.


You must know which address to use to determine the correct rate. There are two different approaches to determining which address to apply:


- **Destination-based sourcing:** Apply the rate where the buyer receives the item. This rule applies in most states and for virtually all remote sales.
- **Origin-based sourcing:** Apply the rate where the seller is located. Arizona, Illinois, Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and Virginia use origin-based sourcing for in-state sellers.


Some states, like California, apply a hybrid rule. You can refer to Numeral’s guide to[origin-based vs. destination-based sourcing](https://www.numeral.com/blog/origin-based-vs-destination-based-sales-tax) to determine which rules apply.


State rules also differ on whether[tax is charged on shipping](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-shipping) , so you will need to understand local requirements.


## Beyond sales tax rates by state: taxability and nexus


Understanding the applicable sales tax rate is just one part of your obligations as a merchant. To determine the correct rate to charge, you also must know:


- Whether you're required to collect sales tax in the state where the sale is made
- Whether the product you are selling is taxable


### Taxability varies by product


Rules differ across jurisdictions regarding when products are subject to sales tax and which items are taxed at the full rate versus a different rate. For example:


- Groceries and clothing are often exempt or taxed at a reduced rate.
- [SaaS](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-saas) and[digital goods](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-on-digital-goods) are sometimes taxable and sometimes exempt depending on the state.
- Wholesale and manufacturing purchases are often exempt as long as the buyer provides a valid[resale or exemption certificate](https://www.numeral.com/blog/resale-certificates) .


### Nexus determines where you collect


You also must know whether you have[nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/sales-tax-nexus) in a particular state to determine if you are required to collect. You can establish:


- [Economic nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/economic-nexus) **:** This means you have sufficient economic connections with the state. Generally, economic nexus is established once you have a certain sales volume or number of transactions (such as $100,000 of sales into the state or 200 transactions).
- [Physical nexus](https://www.numeral.com/blog/physical-nexus) **:** This means you have a local presence in the state, such as a warehouse or storefront.


Before 2018, sellers had to collect sales tax only in locations where they had a physical presence.[South Dakota v. Wayfair](https://www.numeral.com/blog/south-dakota-v-wayfair) changed this rule, opening the door to economic nexus. This added significant complexity for multi-state sellers who may now need to understand sales tax rules and rates across dozens of jurisdictions.
